tips.title: Two sizes, and the ratio between them
tips.body: An atom has a radius of about **$1 \times 10^{-10}$ m**, and the nucleus is **less than 1/10 000** of that — under $1 \times 10^{-14}$ m. Both are stated in the specification, and the **ratio** is what questions usually test.

tips.title: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number
tips.body: **Atomic number** is the **protons**; **mass number** is **protons + neutrons**. So subtract to get neutrons. Carbon-14 has mass number 14 and atomic number 6, giving $14 - 6 = 8$ neutrons.

tips.title: Isotopes differ in neutrons only
tips.body: Atoms of the **same element** always have the **same number of protons** — that is what makes them the same element. **Isotopes** differ only in their **neutrons**, so they have the same atomic number and a different mass number.

tips.title: New evidence changes the model
tips.body: The story runs **evidence → new model**, never the reverse. The plum pudding model was not wrong-headed; it fitted what was known. **Alpha scattering** produced results it could not explain, so it was replaced.

tips.title: Absorb to move out, emit to move in
tips.body: Electrons sit at different distances from the nucleus. **Absorbing** electromagnetic radiation moves an electron **further out**, to a higher energy level; **emitting** it moves the electron **closer in**. Absorb out, emit in.

why.matters:
Everything you can touch is made of about ninety kinds of atom, and this topic is the anatomy of one: a nucleus of protons and neutrons that is almost all the mass and almost none of the size, and electrons around it in fixed energy levels. Two counts, protons and neutrons, are enough to name any atom there is.

It is also the course's clearest case of how science changes its mind. The model of the atom was replaced three times because an experiment said so, and the alpha scattering result is the one to know.

examples.title: The atom as a football pitch
examples.body:
The specification's ratio is worth seeing. The nucleus is less than **1/10 000** of the atom's radius. Scale an atom up until it is a football pitch, about 100 m end to end, and the nucleus is a marble 1 cm across on the centre spot. Everything else, the whole pitch, is the space the electrons move in.

And the marble holds almost all the mass. That pairing, tiny and heavy, is what the alpha particles found: most sailed through the empty pitch, and the rare one that met the marble bounced straight back. Solid-feeling matter is nearly all nothing.

examples.title: Why chlorine weighs 35.5 on the periodic table
examples.body:
Every periodic table gives chlorine a mass of 35.5, and no chlorine atom weighs that. Chlorine comes as two **isotopes**: every atom has 17 protons, which is what makes it chlorine, but some have 18 neutrons and some 20. They are chlorine-35 and chlorine-37, chemically identical, and about three atoms in four are the lighter one.

So the table prints the average of a sample: $0.75 \times 35 + 0.25 \times 37 = 35.5$. A decimal on the periodic table is not a strange atom; it is a mixture of ordinary ones, and the same protons throughout.

examples.title: Why fireworks come in colours
examples.body:
Heat an atom and some of its electrons are knocked up to higher energy levels. They cannot stay. Each falls back to a lower level and, as the specification puts it, **emits electromagnetic radiation** as it does. The energy of that radiation is the gap between the two levels, and for visible gaps that energy is a colour.

Every element has its own set of levels, so its own set of gaps, so its own colours. A firework maker chooses the metal for the colour. The colour you see in the sky is the ladder of energy levels inside one kind of atom.

boxes.body: The burning firework knocks electrons up to higher energy levels.

boxes.title: Fall
boxes.body: Each electron drops back to a lower level and emits electromagnetic radiation.

boxes.title: Colour
boxes.body: The radiation's energy is the size of the gap, and a visible gap is a colour.

boxes.body: Each element has its own gaps, so its own colours: the firework maker picks the metal.

steps.title: The structure of an atom
steps.body:
**Atoms are very small**, with a radius of about **$1 \times 10^{-10}$ metres**. That is one ten-billionth of a metre, and it is a figure the specification asks you to recognise in standard form.

**The basic structure** is a **positively charged nucleus composed of both protons and neutrons**, surrounded by **negatively charged electrons**.

**The nucleus is extraordinarily small compared with the atom.** Its radius is **less than 1/10 000 of the radius of an atom** — under $1 \times 10^{-14}$ m. Almost all of an atom is empty space.

**Yet most of the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus.** Protons and neutrons are far more massive than electrons, so nearly all the mass sits in that tiny central volume.

**Putting the two facts together** is the point: the nucleus is **tiny but heavy**. If an atom were scaled up to the size of a football stadium, the nucleus would be a pea at the centre — and that pea would carry almost the whole mass.

**The electrons are arranged at different distances from the nucleus**, at what are called **different energy levels**.

**Those arrangements can change.** An electron that **absorbs electromagnetic radiation** moves **further from the nucleus**, to a **higher** energy level. One that **emits electromagnetic radiation** moves **closer to the nucleus**, to a **lower** energy level. Absorbing takes energy in and lifts the electron out; emitting gives energy away and lets it fall back.

steps.title: Atomic number, mass number and isotopes
steps.body:
**Counting the particles is what these terms are for.**

**In an atom the number of electrons is equal to the number of protons**, so **atoms have no overall electrical charge** — the positive and negative charges balance exactly.

**All atoms of a particular element have the same number of protons.** That is what makes them that element. The number of protons is called the **atomic number**.

**The total number of protons and neutrons** in an atom is called the **mass number**.

**So neutrons are found by subtracting:**

$$\text{neutrons} = \text{mass number} - \text{atomic number}$$

**Isotopes.** *Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; these atoms are called **isotopes** of that element.* They have the **same atomic number** and a **different mass number**.

Carbon always has **6 protons**. Carbon-12 has a mass number of 12, so $12 - 6 = 6$ neutrons. Carbon-14 has a mass number of 14, so $14 - 6 = 8$ neutrons. Same element, two extra neutrons.

**Ions.** *Atoms turn into **positive ions** if they **lose one or more outer electrons**.* Losing a negative electron leaves the atom with more protons than electrons, so it now carries a **positive** charge. Note the specification says **lose** — gaining electrons is not mentioned here.

steps.title: How the model changed
steps.body:
**New experimental evidence may lead to a scientific model being changed or replaced.** That sentence is the point of this whole section — it is about how science works, not only about atoms.

**Before the electron was discovered**, atoms were thought to be **tiny spheres that could not be divided**.

**The discovery of the electron led to the plum pudding model**, which suggested the atom is **a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it**. This was a reasonable model: it accounted for the electron and kept the atom neutral overall.

**Then came the alpha particle scattering experiment.** Its **results led to the conclusion that the mass of an atom was concentrated at the centre (the nucleus), and that the nucleus was charged**. This **nuclear model replaced the plum pudding model**.

**Niels Bohr adapted the nuclear model** by suggesting that **electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances**. His theoretical **calculations agreed with experimental observations**, which is why the adaptation was accepted — agreement with measurement is what settles it.

**Later experiments** led to the idea that the positive charge of any nucleus could be **subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles, each with the same amount of positive charge**. These were named **protons**.

**The experimental work of James Chadwick provided the evidence** for **neutrons** within the nucleus — about **20 years after the nucleus itself was accepted**.

**Notice the pattern throughout:** each change was forced by **evidence**, and each new model kept what the old one explained while accounting for something more.

steps.title: Energy levels and electrons
steps.body:
**The electrons are arranged at different distances from the nucleus**, and those distances correspond to **different energy levels**.

**The arrangement can change**, and the specification is precise about how:

- **absorbing** electromagnetic radiation moves an electron **further from the nucleus**, to a **higher** energy level
- **emitting** electromagnetic radiation moves an electron **closer to the nucleus**, to a **lower** energy level

**Absorb out, emit in.** Absorbing radiation supplies energy, and it takes energy to move away from the attraction of the positive nucleus. Emitting radiation gives energy away, so the electron falls back closer in.

**This is Bohr's contribution in practice.** He proposed that electrons orbit at **specific distances** rather than anywhere at all — which means only **particular** energy changes are possible, namely the gaps between those levels.

**Why Bohr's model was accepted** is worth stating in the specification's own terms: his **theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations**. A model is not adopted because it sounds sensible, but because its predictions match what is measured.

**Connecting to ionisation.** If an electron absorbs enough energy it can leave the atom altogether. The atom has then **lost an electron** and become a **positive ion**, which links this section directly to the ionising effect of radiation in the next topic.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Give both sizes and the ratio.** An atom is about **$1 \times 10^{-10}$ m**; the nucleus is **less than 1/10 000** of that radius. The ratio is what makes the point — the atom is **mostly empty space**, yet the nucleus holds **almost all the mass**.

**Hold "tiny" and "heavy" together.** A common half-answer says the nucleus is very small, or that it holds most of the mass, but not both. The two facts together are what alpha scattering established.

**Subtract for neutrons.** Mass number **minus** atomic number. Adding them, or confusing which is which, is the commonest arithmetic slip here.

**Define isotopes by neutrons only.** Same element means the **same number of protons** — and therefore the same atomic number. Isotopes differ **only** in neutrons, so only the **mass number** changes.

**Tell the alpha scattering story through the anomaly.** *Most passed through* shows empty space, and on its own fits either model. *A very few bounced back* is the observation the plum pudding model **could not explain**, because a diffuse positive charge could never repel a fast alpha particle that strongly. Naming which observation was fatal, and why, is the difference between describing the experiment and explaining it.

**Say why Bohr was accepted** in the specification's terms: his **theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations**. Not because the idea was elegant — because it matched measurement.

**Get the order and the credit right.** Indivisible spheres → plum pudding (after the **electron**) → nuclear (after **alpha scattering**) → Bohr (specific orbits). **Protons** came from the discovery that nuclear charge is a whole number of equal parts; **Chadwick** provided the evidence for **neutrons**, about **20 years** after the nucleus.

**Use this as evidence about how science works.** **New experimental evidence may lead to a model being changed or replaced.** The plum pudding model was not foolish — it fitted what was known at the time, and was abandoned when it stopped fitting. Saying that explicitly is what a top answer does with a "describe how the model developed" question.

**Absorb out, emit in.** Absorbing electromagnetic radiation moves an electron to a **higher** level further out; emitting moves it **closer in**. Getting this backwards is easy and costly.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- An atom has a radius of about **$1 \times 10^{-10}$ m**.
- The **nucleus** contains **protons and neutrons** and is **positively charged**.
- Its radius is **less than 1/10 000** of the atom's radius.
- **Almost all the mass** of an atom is in the nucleus.
- **Electrons** are negative and sit at different distances — **energy levels**.
- **Absorbing** EM radiation moves an electron **further out**; **emitting** moves it **closer in**.
- **Number of electrons = number of protons**, so atoms have **no overall charge**.
- **Atomic number** = number of **protons**; all atoms of an element share it.
- **Mass number** = **protons + neutrons**.
- **Neutrons = mass number − atomic number.**
- **Isotopes** are atoms of the same element with **different numbers of neutrons**.
- Atoms become **positive ions** by **losing** outer electrons.
- Models in order: **indivisible spheres → plum pudding → nuclear → Bohr**.
- **Alpha scattering** replaced plum pudding with the **nuclear** model.
- **Chadwick** provided the evidence for **neutrons**, about 20 years later.

questions.prompt: Describe how the model of the atom developed, from indivisible spheres to the Bohr model, explaining what evidence caused each change.
questions.solution:
**Before the electron was discovered**, atoms were thought to be **tiny spheres that could not be divided**. There was no evidence of anything inside them, so there was nothing for a model to describe.

**The discovery of the electron changed that.** If a negatively charged particle could come out of an atom, the atom must have parts. This led to the **plum pudding model**, which suggested that the atom is **a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it**. This was a sound model for its evidence: it accounted for the electron and kept the atom neutral overall.

**The alpha particle scattering experiment overturned it.** Alpha particles were fired at a very thin sheet of gold foil and their paths recorded. Three things were seen.

**Most passed straight through**, showing the atom is largely **empty space**. On its own this fits either model, so it settles nothing. **Some were deflected** through noticeable angles, showing they had passed near a **concentration of positive charge**, since alpha particles are positive and are repelled. **A very few bounced back** almost the way they had come.

That last observation was **fatal to the plum pudding model**. A diffuse, spread-out ball of positive charge could never repel a fast alpha particle strongly enough to reverse it. To turn one back, the positive charge must be **concentrated into a very small volume**, and that volume must carry **most of the atom's mass** — otherwise it would simply be knocked aside.

So the results **led to the conclusion that the mass of an atom was concentrated at the centre, in a charged nucleus**, and this **nuclear model replaced the plum pudding model**.

**Niels Bohr then adapted the nuclear model** by suggesting that **electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances** rather than anywhere at all. His model was accepted for a specific reason worth stating: his **theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations**.

**Later refinements followed.** Experiments showed the positive charge of any nucleus could be **subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles of equal positive charge**, which were named **protons**. Roughly **20 years** after the nucleus was accepted, the experimental work of **James Chadwick** provided the evidence for **neutrons** within it.

**What the whole sequence shows** is how science works: **new experimental evidence may lead to a scientific model being changed or replaced**. None of the earlier models was foolish — each fitted the evidence available when it was proposed, and each was revised when new observations no longer fitted. A model is judged by whether its predictions match measurement, which is exactly why Bohr's agreement with observation was what secured his.

Holding both facts together is the important part: the nucleus is **tiny but heavy**. Scaled to a football stadium, the nucleus would be a pea at the centre carrying almost the entire mass.

The **electrons are arranged at different distances from the nucleus**, at different **energy levels**. An electron that **absorbs** electromagnetic radiation moves to a **higher** level further out; one that **emits** it moves **closer in**.

**The atomic number is the number of protons.** All atoms of a particular element have the **same** number of protons — that is what makes them that element — so the atomic number identifies the element.

**The mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons.** Since it counts both, the neutrons are found by **subtraction**:

$$\text{neutrons} = \text{mass number} - \text{atomic number}$$

In a neutral atom **the number of electrons equals the number of protons**, so the positive and negative charges balance and the **atom has no overall electrical charge**.

**Isotopes** are **atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons**. Because the element is the same, the **number of protons — and so the atomic number — is unchanged**; only the **mass number** differs.

Carbon illustrates this. Every carbon atom has **6 protons**. Carbon-12 has a mass number of 12, so it has $12 - 6 = \mathbf{6}$ neutrons. Carbon-14 has a mass number of 14, so it has $14 - 6 = \mathbf{8}$ neutrons. Both have 6 protons and, when neutral, 6 electrons — so both are carbon, and both are electrically neutral. They differ by two neutrons alone.

**Ions** are different again. **Atoms turn into positive ions if they lose one or more outer electrons.** Losing a negative electron leaves the atom with **more protons than electrons**, so it carries a net **positive** charge. Note that this changes the **electrons**, not the nucleus — so an ion is still the same element, with the same atomic number, and is not a different isotope.

examTechnique.body:
Give the **sizes and the ratio**: an atom is about $1 \times 10^{-10}$ m and the nucleus is **less than 1/10 000** of that — yet holds **almost all the mass**.

**Neutrons = mass number − atomic number.** For alpha scattering, name the observation the old model **could not explain** and say why. Say Bohr was accepted because his **calculations agreed with observations**.
examinerErrors: Saying the nucleus is small, or heavy, but not both.
Adding the mass number and atomic number instead of subtracting.
Defining isotopes without specifying that only neutrons differ.
Listing alpha scattering observations without saying which was fatal.
Saying the plum pudding model was simply wrong or careless.
Swapping absorption and emission of radiation by electrons.
Crediting Chadwick with the proton rather than the neutron.
Saying a positive ion has gained electrons.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer gives **both** sizes and the **ratio**, and holds the two facts together: the nucleus is **tiny** and carries **almost all the mass**. It subtracts to find neutrons and defines **isotopes** by the neutron count alone, keeping them distinct from **ions**, which differ in electrons. On alpha scattering it does not merely list observations but identifies **which one the plum pudding model could not survive** — the few that bounced back — and explains why a diffuse charge could not do that. It states that Bohr was accepted because his **calculations agreed with experimental observations**, and it draws the wider point the specification is making: **new evidence changes or replaces a model**, and the older models fitted the evidence of their time.
